newsitem.title: USA: Supreme Court blocks California man's execution.
newsitem.headline: Supreme Court blocks California man's execution.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court blocked the execution of convicted killer Thomas Thompson on Monday a few hours before he had been scheduled to die at San Quentin State Prison.
"There'll be no execution tonight," a Supreme Court spokeswoman said. She said the court would hear arguments about the controversial case when it resumed work in October.

Thompson had said goodbye to visiting friends and relatives and was about to be moved to the deathwatch cell when word came from Washington that the execution would definitely not go ahead, prison officials said.

He had ordered his last meal -- spinach salad, Alaskan king crab legs with butter, Mandarin-style spare ribs with pork and fried rice, a hot fudge sundae and a six-pack of Coca-Cola -- but did not receive it because it had not been prepared, a prison spokeswoman said.

Thompson, now 42, was convicted in 1983 of raping and murdering Ginger Fleischli, 20, two years earlier at his apartment in Laguna Beach in Southern California after an evening of drinking and smoking hashish. He has protested his innocence, saying he passed out after consensual sex with Fleischli.
A federal appeals court threw out Thompson's death sentence and reversed his rape conviction Sunday, stopping his execution, which had been scheduled for soon after midnight on Monday.

The appeals court raised doubts about the rape conviction and criticised his trial attorney for failing to undermine the testimony of two jailhouse informants who said Thompson had admitted his guilt to them.
The rape conviction was a "special circumstance" that in combination with murder made Thompson eligible for the death penalty under California law.
The state appealed to the Supreme Court to overturn the ruling and allow the execution to go ahead as planned.
The Supreme Court refused to reverse the appeals court decision but said it would review the merits of the case when it began work in October after its summer break, a court spokeswoman said.
She said the Supreme Court would hear arguments about the appeals court's surprise decision to review the Thompson case.
Thompson, who had been scheduled to die by lethal injection, would have been the fifth person put to death in California since the state resumed executions in 1992.

Procedures went on throughout the day at San Quentin as though the execution would go ahead. The prison was placed on lockdown, with prisoners confined to their cells, and access roads to the institution were closed. Some death penalty protesters marched to the prison.

California Attorney General Dan Lungren lambasted the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday evening, saying its ruling was inexplicable. "It sends a message to the victims that justice delayed is tough luck for you," he told a news conference in Sacramento. He voiced hope that the Supreme Court would put an end to the "9th Circuit circus."
The appeals court decision also outraged Republican Gov. Pete Wilson, who on Sunday blamed it on a "coterie of liberal judges."
In 1995 a U.S. District Court judge, finding that Thompson had been inadequately represented by his attorney at his trial, threw out the rape conviction and death sentence.

But the conviction and sentence were reinstated by a three-judge panel of the 9th Circuit Court. The Supreme Court denied Thompson's appeal, Wilson denied his clemency plea, and all hope for Thompson seemed lost.
But in a surprise move, an 11-judge panel of the 9th Circuit Court, which has a liberal reputation, reviewed the case and overturned the earlier ruling.
